title: A Renowned Scholar's Immersive Week of Directing AI with Pure Voice Commands

content_html:
Recently, Azeem Azhar, a renowned technology observer and founder of Exponential View, accidentally left his laptop at his home in Amsterdam while traveling to London. This accident led him to conduct a one-week real-world experiment of "voice-only office work," offering him a groundbreaking new understanding of the future of human-computer interaction.

For a long time, modern office work has revolved around computer screens and keyboards. Whether handling Slack messages, writing Word documents, or creating Excel models, people have subconsciously assumed that "sitting at a desk and typing" is the only correct way to work. However, during this week, Azhar discovered that this office tradition, built over decades, is quietly beginning to loosen and may soon disappear completely.

The core of this office work transformation is the GPT-Live feature previously released by OpenAI. It allows users to directly command AI agents in the background to complete complex digital tasks through voice commands. In practice, this system feels like the super assistant Jarvis from Iron Man, seamlessly operating various digital tools.

During the week without his laptop, Azhar did not squint at small text on his phone screen or suffer neck pain from looking down at the screen. Instead, he communicated in real-time with ChatGPT on his phone entirely through voice. Using the natural interaction method of "speaking and receiving feedback," he successfully completed most of the core tasks of his daily work.

This accidental minimalistic business trip not only confirmed the feasibility of voice-driven AI agents handling daily work but also clearly reflected the evolving trend of future productivity. As underlying technologies continue to mature, screens and keyboards may no longer be the only bridge connecting us to the digital world. Humans are accelerating toward a new era of collaboration deeply empowered by voice and advanced AI agents.
